To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the wrapping mimicking concept can be applied to protein‐protein interfaces, and that the small molecules that disrupt such interfaces do in fact mimic the wrapping behavior of their protein partners.

(i) the wrapping behavior of a small molecule disruptive of protein– protein interactions is a key feature of the binding mode; (ii) this wrapping mimicking behavior is not limited to a specific type of protein–protein complex, but it is a general phenomenon; (iii) this wrapping mimiking is a consequence of the fact that the small molecule binds in the interface of the complex and replaces the natural protein partner; (iv) the wrapping behavior is not a mere consequence of the chemical similarity

(i) the disruptive drug‐like small‐molecule binding sites are located in regions of the target protein where the natural protein partner is involved in wrapping interactions with the target protein; (ii) the small‐molecule residues in these regions are located in positions that are very close to those of the residues in the protein partner involved in the wrapping interactions; and (iii) the small‐ molecule residues have the same chemical character as the protein partner residues.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of protein–protein binding hot spots, the identification and characterization of protein binding interfaces and the analysis of the role of protein–protein wrapping interactions in the binding process.
the study of the protein–protein interactions (PPI) and the role of the nonpolar groups of proteins in the PPIs.
the study of the wrapping behavior in protein–protein interfaces and the role it plays in the binding process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the complexes analyzed in this work, the disruptive small molecule mimics the wrapping behavior of its replaced protein partner.
the small molecules mimic in a very significant manner the wrapping behavior of their protein partner.

the small molecules we studied in this work are able to replace the natural protein partners in the protein complexes by performing a wrapping behavior that is in some way similar to the wrapping of the natural partner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show the importance of wrapping mimicking for successful disruptive small molecules.
small disruptive molecules can be designed by mimicking the wrapping behavior of their protein targets.
the small molecules disrupt protein–protein interactions by mimicking to a great extent their natural protein partners in the wrapping of the binding interfaces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
small‐molecule disruptive drugs of protein–protein interaction can mimic the wrapping behavior of proteins in the complex interface.
disruptive small‐molecules can be seen as mimicking the behavior of the partner protein in wrapping the target protein.
the small molecule disrupts protein–protein interfaces by mimicking the wrapping interactions of the partner protein, thus providing a physical meaning to the concept of mimicking.
